title: How We Build Effective Agents: Barry Zhang, Anthropic
talk_summary: Barry Zhang argues agents should only be built for ambiguous, high-value, verifiable tasks, and that the core agent loop (environment, tools, system prompt) should stay simple while iterating. He also urges builders to 'think like your agent' by inspecting the limited context window the model actually sees, and flags budget-awareness and multi-agent context isolation as key open problems.

takeaways.technique: Workflow-vs-agent checklist before spawning an agent
takeaways.what_they_do: Before building an agent, they check task complexity, task value, whether critical capabilities are de-risked, and cost of error/error discovery; if the decision tree is mappable, they build an explicit workflow instead.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you can map out the entire decision tree pretty easily, just build that explicitly and then optimize every node
takeaways.numbers: 10-cent budget per task affords only 30-50k tokens

takeaways.technique: Think like your agent: audit the actual context window
takeaways.what_they_do: They put themselves in the agent's 10-20k token context and ask whether it is sufficient and coherent; they also feed system prompts and trajectories back to a model asking where instructions are ambiguous or what context is missing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Everything that the model knows about the current state of the world is going to be explained in that 10 to 20k tokens.

takeaways.technique: Sub-agents to protect the main context window
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue multi-agent setups work because they parallelize well, separate concerns, and a sub-agent protects the main agent's context window.
takeaways.evidence_quote: having sub agent for example will really protect the main agents context window

takeaways.what_they_do: They identify lack of cost/latency control in agents as a top open problem and ask how to define and enforce budgets in time, money, and tokens.
takeaways.evidence_quote: what's the best way to define and enforce budgets in terms of time, in terms of money, in terms of tokens

takeaways.what_they_do: They throw tool descriptions and system prompts into a model to check whether the agent knows how to use the tool, wants more/fewer parameters, or finds instructions ambiguous.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You can throw in a two description and see whether the agent knows how to use the tool.

takeaways.technique: Prefer tasks with verifiable outputs (unit tests/CI)
takeaways.what_they_do: They explain coding is a strong agent use case partly because output is easily verifiable through unit tests and CI, which supports trusting autonomy.
takeaways.evidence_quote: coding has this really nice property where the output is easily verifiable through unit test and CI
